The key technique is completing the square to convert back to standard form, which also reveals special cases such as a point circle or an empty set. A quick checklist helps students identify the centre and radius or determine that the equation is not a circle.

data.prerequisites: Students should already know how to work with squares, square roots, and the distance formula in the coordinate plane.
why: Circles model many real‑world objects such as wheels, satellite orbits, and lenses. Being able to write their equations lets engineers design parts that fit together precisely.
In navigation and computer graphics, circles are used to calculate ranges, collision zones, and to render smooth curves. Understanding circle equations is a foundation for these applications.

sections.heading: 1. Review: Distance Formula and Centre‑Radius Description
sections.body:
The idea of a circle is simple: it is the set of all points that are exactly the same distance from a single fixed point.  
That fixed point is called the **centre** of the circle and we usually write it as the ordered pair \((h,k)\).  
The common distance that every point on the circle shares with the centre is called the **radius**, denoted by \(r\).

> **Definition:** A circle with centre \((h,k)\) and radius \(r\) is the collection of all points \((x,y)\) such that the distance between \((x,y)\) and \((h,k)\) equals \(r\).

To work with circles algebraically we need a way to measure the distance between two points in the plane.  
If you have two points \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\), you can think of the line segment joining them as the hypotenuse of a right‑angled triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical differences between the points.  
By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of that hypotenuse is

$$
\text{distance}= \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}.
$$

This is the **distance formula**. It tells us exactly how far apart any two points are.

Now apply the distance formula to the centre \((h,k)\) and an arbitrary point \((x,y)\) on the circle.  
Because every point on the circle is exactly \(r\) units from the centre, we set the distance equal to \(r\):

$$
\sqrt{(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2}=r.
$$

If we square both sides (which removes the square‑root and keeps the equality true because both sides are non‑negative), we obtain the **centre‑radius description** of a circle:

$$
(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2 = r^{2}.
$$

This equation is called the **standard form** of a circle, and it is very useful because the numbers \(h\), \(k\), and \(r\) appear directly in the formula.  
Reading the equation tells you the centre and the radius immediately, without any extra work.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a round table. The centre of the table is the point \((h,k)\). If you place a cup anywhere on the edge, the distance from the cup to the centre is always the same—the radius of the table. The equation above is just a mathematical way of saying “stay on the edge”.

Why do we square the equation? Squaring eliminates the square‑root, which is hard to manipulate algebraically, and it turns the relationship into a polynomial equation. This makes it easier to combine with other algebraic expressions later on, such as when we expand to the general form or complete the square.

> **Note:** When you square both sides, you must keep the original condition that \(r\ge 0\). The radius is a length, so it can never be negative.

A quick check helps you see the formula in action. Suppose the centre is \((2, -3)\) and the radius is \(5\). Plugging these numbers into the standard form gives

$$
(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2 = 25.
$$

If you pick a point, say \((7,-3)\), and substitute it into the left‑hand side, you get \((7-2)^2+( -3+3)^2 = 5^2+0 = 25\), which matches the right‑hand side. Hence \((7,-3)\) lies on the circle, as expected because it is exactly five units to the right of the centre.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting the signs inside the parentheses. The term \((x-h)\) means “subtract the centre’s x‑coordinate from the point’s x‑coordinate”. If the centre’s x‑coordinate is negative, the expression becomes \((x-(-h)) = (x+h)\). Write the signs carefully to avoid errors.

Remember that the distance formula works for any two points, not just for a centre and a point on a circle. Whenever you see a problem that asks for the distance between two locations—say, between two houses on a map—you can use the same formula.

> **Remember:** The centre‑radius description \((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^{2}\) is just the distance formula applied to a centre \((h,k)\) and a point \((x,y)\) on the circle, with the distance set equal to the radius \(r\). This compact equation is the foundation for everything we will do with circles in the rest of the lesson.

sections.heading: 2. Standard Form of a Circle
sections.body:
The equation  

$$ (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2 $$  

is called the **standard form** of a circle.  
It tells us everything we need to know about a circle in the coordinate plane:

* **$(h,k)$** is the **centre** – the point that is exactly in the middle of the circle.  
* **$r$** is the **radius** – the distance from the centre to any point on the edge of the circle.  

Why does this work?  
Recall the **distance formula**: the distance between two points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is  

$$ d = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}. $$  

If a point $(x,y)$ lies on a circle whose centre is $(h,k)$, then the distance from $(x,y)$ to $(h,k)$ must equal the radius $r$.  
Squaring both sides of the distance formula removes the square‑root and gives exactly the standard form above.  
Writing the equation this way is useful because the centre and radius are read off directly – no extra algebra is needed.

> **Definition:** The **standard form** of a circle is $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$, where $(h,k)$ is the centre and $r$ is the radius.

> **In daily life:** Think of a round swimming pool. The centre $(h,k)$ is the middle of the pool floor, and the radius $r$ is how far you can swim from the middle before you reach the edge.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting the signs inside the parentheses. The term $(x-h)$ means “subtract the $h$‑coordinate of the centre from $x$”. If the centre’s $x$‑coordinate is negative, the expression becomes $(x-(-3)) = (x+3)$. Write the signs exactly as shown; otherwise the centre will be read incorrectly.

---

### Example 1 (Easy): Write the equation of a circle with centre \((3,-2)\) and radius \(5\).

1. Identify the centre \((h,k)\).  
   Here \(h = 3\) and \(k = -2\).  

2. Identify the radius \(r\).  
   The radius is given as \(r = 5\).  

3. Substitute \(h\), \(k\) and \(r\) into the standard form.  

$$ (x-3)^2 + (y-(-2))^2 = 5^2 $$  

4. Simplify the double negative inside the second parentheses.  

$$ (x-3)^2 + (y+2)^2 = 25 $$  

**Answer:** The equation is \((x-3)^2 + (y+2)^2 = 25\).

---

The standard form also lets us **read** the centre and radius from an equation that is already written in that shape.  

### Example 2 (Easy): Find the centre and radius of \((x-4)^2 + (y+1)^2 = 9\).

1. Compare the given equation with the template \((x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2\).  

2. The first term is \((x-4)^2\); therefore \(h = 4\).  

3. The second term is \((y+1)^2\).  Because the template has \((y-k)\), we rewrite \(y+1\) as \(y-(-1)\).  
   Hence \(k = -1\).  

4. The right‑hand side is \(9\), which is \(r^2\).  
   Take the square root: \(r = \sqrt{9} = 3\).  

**Answer:** The centre is \((4,-1)\) and the radius is \(3\).

---

Once the centre and radius are known, many other tasks become simple: plotting the circle, checking whether a point lies on it, or converting to the **general form** later in the lesson.  

> **Remember:** In the standard form, the signs inside the parentheses are opposite to the coordinates of the centre.  
> • If the centre’s $x$‑coordinate is positive, write $(x-h)$.  
> • If the centre’s $x$‑coordinate is negative, write $(x-(-h)) = (x+h)$.  
> The same rule holds for the $y$‑coordinate.

By mastering this compact notation, you can move quickly between geometric ideas (a circle drawn on paper) and algebraic work (solving equations). The next sections will show how to expand the formula to the general form and how to reverse the process with completing the square.

sections.heading: 3. Expanding to General Form
sections.body:
When we have a circle written in the **centre‑radius description**  

\[
(x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2},
\]

the symbols $h$ and $k$ tell us exactly where the centre is, and $r$ tells us how far every point on the circle is from that centre.  
Sometimes, however, the equation we meet in a textbook or a word problem does **not** look like this.  
It may be written as a single polynomial set equal to zero, for example  

\[
Ax^{2}+Ay^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0 .
\]

This is called the **general form** of a circle.  
Converting from the centre‑radius description to the general form is useful because:

* It lets us recognise a circle even when the centre and radius are hidden.
* It makes it easy to combine the circle equation with other algebraic equations (e.g., lines) when solving systems.
* Many computer‑algebra systems output circles in general form, so we need to be able to read them.

The conversion is simply a matter of expanding the squares and moving every term to one side of the equation.

> **Note:** In the general form the coefficients of $x^{2}$ and $y^{2}$ are always the same (both called $A$). If they differ, the curve is an ellipse, not a circle.

---

### Expanding step‑by‑step

Take the centre‑radius equation  

\[
(x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}.
\]

1. **Square each binomial** – use the identity $(a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}$.  
2. **Distribute** the $2ab$ term carefully, remembering the sign of $h$ and $k$.  
3. **Move** the constant $r^{2}$ to the left side so that the right side becomes $0$.  
4. **Collect** like terms: all $x^{2}$ terms together, all $y^{2}$ terms together, and the linear $x$ and $y$ terms.

The result will match the pattern  

\[
Ax^{2}+Ay^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0,
\]

where  

* $A=1$ (because the coefficient of $x^{2}$ and $y^{2}$ comes from expanding the squares),  
* $D=-2h$, $E=-2k$, and  
* $F=h^{2}+k^{2}-r^{2}$.

> **Remember:** The signs of $D$ and $E$ are opposite the signs of $h$ and $k$ because the expansion produces $-2hx$ and $-2ky$.

---

**Example 3 (Medium): Expand \((x-2)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=16\) to general form.**  

We start with a circle whose centre is $(2,-3)$ and radius $4$ (since $r^{2}=16$).

1. **Square the binomials.**  
   $$ (x-2)^{2}=x^{2}-4x+4, \qquad (y+3)^{2}=y^{2}+6y+9. $$
2. **Add the two results and set equal to $16$.**  
   $$ x^{2}-4x+4 \;+\; y^{2}+6y+9 \;=\; 16. $$
3. **Combine constants on the left and move $16$ to the left side.**  
   $$ x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+6y+13-16=0 $$  
   $$ x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+6y-3=0. $$

**Answer:** The general form is  

\[
\boxed{x^{2}+y^{2}-4x+6y-3=0},
\]

so $A=1$, $D=-4$, $E=6$, $F=-3$.

---

Now that we can go from centre‑radius to general form, we also need the reverse: starting with a general‑form equation and **recovering** the centre and radius. This is done by **completing the square**, which we will see in the next section. Before that, let’s practise the reverse direction.

**Example 4 (Medium): Given \(x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+8y-11=0\), rewrite it in standard form and state the centre and radius.**  

The equation is already in general form, so we must group the $x$‑terms and $y$‑terms and complete the square for each.

1. **Group like terms.**  
   $$ (x^{2}-6x) \;+\; (y^{2}+8y) \;-\; 11 = 0. $$
2. **Complete the square for the $x$‑group.**  
   Take half of the coefficient of $x$, which is $-6$, giving $-3$. Square it: $(-3)^{2}=9$. Add and subtract $9$ inside the group:  
   $$ (x^{2}-6x+9) - 9. $$
   Similarly for the $y$‑group: half of $8$ is $4$, $4^{2}=16$. Add and subtract $16$:  
   $$ (y^{2}+8y+16) - 16. $$
   Substituting back, we have  
   $$ (x^{2}-6x+9) + (y^{2}+8y+16) - 9 - 16 - 11 = 0. $$
3. **Rewrite each completed square as a binomial squared and move constants to the right.**  
   $$ (x-3)^{2} + (y+4)^{2} = 9+16+11 $$  
   $$ (x-3)^{2} + (y+4)^{2} = 36. $$

**Answer:** The standard (centre‑radius) form is  

\[
\boxed{(x-3)^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=36},
\]

so the centre is $(3,-4)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{36}=6$ units.

> **In daily life:** Think of the general form as a “packed suitcase” – all the information about where the circle sits and how big it is is hidden inside the coefficients. Expanding or unpacking (by completing the square) lets you see the centre and radius, just like opening the suitcase reveals the clothes inside.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to move the constant term $r^{2}$ to the left side when forming the general equation. This leaves a non‑zero right‑hand side and prevents the equation from matching the $Ax^{2}+Ay^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0$ pattern.

Now you can freely move between the two ways of writing a circle. This flexibility will be essential when solving intersection problems or modelling real‑world situations where the circle’s centre is not given directly.

sections.heading: 4. Completing the Square to Find Centre and Radius
sections.body:
When we are given a circle equation in **general form**  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0,
\]

the numbers \(D,E,F\) hide the centre and the radius.  
To reveal them we *complete the square* for the \(x\)-terms and the \(y\)-terms.  

> **Definition:** *Completing the square* means rewriting a quadratic expression \(ax^{2}+bx\) as a perfect square \((x+h)^{2}\) plus (or minus) a constant.  
> **Note:** This technique works because a perfect square expands to a quadratic with the same \(x^{2}\) and \(x\) coefficients, so we can match the original expression.

---

### Why completing the square helps

Think of the circle’s equation as a recipe. The ingredients \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are always present, but the linear parts \(Dx\) and \(Ey\) are like extra spices that shift the centre away from the origin. By grouping the \(x\)-terms together and the \(y\)-terms together, then turning each group into a perfect square, we isolate the “shift” (the centre) and the leftover constant becomes the radius squared.

---

### Step‑by‑step procedure

1. **Group** the \(x\)-terms and the \(y\)-terms.  
   Write the equation as  
   \[
   (x^{2}+Dx)+(y^{2}+Ey)+F=0 .
   \]

2. **Complete the square** for each group.  
   For the \(x\)-group, add and subtract \(\left(\frac{D}{2}\right)^{2}\); for the \(y\)-group, add and subtract \(\left(\frac{E}{2}\right)^{2}\).  
   This gives  
   \[
   \bigl(x^{2}+Dx+\bigl(\tfrac{D}{2}\bigr)^{2}\bigr)
   +\bigl(y^{2}+Ey+\bigl(\tfrac{E}{2}\bigr)^{2}\bigr)
   +F-\bigl(\tfrac{D}{2}\bigr)^{2}-\bigl(\tfrac{E}{2}\bigr)^{2}=0 .
   \]

3. **Rewrite** each completed square as a binomial squared:  
   \[
   (x+\tfrac{D}{2})^{2}+(y+\tfrac{E}{2})^{2}= \bigl(\tfrac{D}{2}\bigr)^{2}+\bigl(\tfrac{E}{2}\bigr)^{2}-F .
   \]

4. **Identify** the centre \((h,k)\) and the radius \(r\).  
   The centre is \((-D/2,\,-E/2)\) and the radius satisfies \(r^{2}= (D/2)^{2}+(E/2)^{2}-F\).  
   If the right‑hand side is positive, \(r=\sqrt{(D/2)^{2}+(E/2)^{2}-F}\); otherwise the equation does **not** represent a real circle.

> **Remember:** The sign of the centre coordinates is opposite to the signs of \(D\) and \(E\) because we move the linear terms to the other side of the equation.

---

### Worked example 1  

**Example 5 (Hard): Convert \(2x^{2}+2y^{2}-12x+8y+10=0\) into standard form.**

1. **Divide** by the common factor \(2\) so the coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) become \(1\).  
   $$
   x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+4y+5=0 .
   $$

2. **Group** the \(x\) and \(y\) parts.  
   $$
   (x^{2}-6x)+(y^{2}+4y)+5=0 .
   $$

3. **Complete the square** for each group.  
   - For \(x^{2}-6x\) add and subtract \((\frac{-6}{2})^{2}=9\).  
   - For \(y^{2}+4y\) add and subtract \((\frac{4}{2})^{2}=4\).  

   $$
   (x^{2}-6x+9)+(y^{2}+4y+4)+5-9-4=0 .
   $$

4. **Rewrite** as squares and simplify the constant side.  
   $$
   (x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=8 .
   $$

5. **Read off** centre and radius.  
   Centre \((h,k)=(3,-2)\); radius \(r=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}\).

**Answer:** The circle in standard form is \((x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=8\) with centre \((3,-2)\) and radius \(2\sqrt{2}\).

---

### Worked example 2  

**Example 6 (Hard): A circle passes through \((1,2)\) and \((4,6)\) and has centre on the line \(y=x\). Find its equation.**

1. **Let** the centre be \((h,k)\). Because it lies on \(y=x\), we have \(k=h\).  
   So the centre is \((h,h)\).

2. **Use the distance formula** to express that both given points are the same distance \(r\) from the centre.  
   For \((1,2)\):  
   $$
   r^{2}=(1-h)^{2}+(2-h)^{2}.
   $$  
   For \((4,6)\):  
   $$
   r^{2}=(4-h)^{2}+(6-h)^{2}.
   $$

3. **Set the two expressions equal** (they both equal \(r^{2}\)) and solve for \(h\).  
   $$
   (1-h)^{2}+(2-h)^{2}=(4-h)^{2}+(6-h)^{2}.
   $$  
   Expand:  
   $$
   (h^{2}-2h+1)+(h^{2}-4h+4)=(h^{2}-8h+16)+(h^{2}-12h+36).
   $$  
   Combine like terms:  
   $$
   2h^{2}-6h+5 = 2h^{2}-20h+52 .
   $$  
   Subtract \(2h^{2}\) from both sides and bring terms together:  
   $$
   -6h+5 = -20h+52 .
   $$  
   Add \(20h\) to each side:  
   $$
   14h+5 = 52 .
   $$  
   Subtract \(5\):  
   $$
   14h = 47 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad h = \frac{47}{14}.
   $$  
   Hence the centre is \(\displaystyle\left(\frac{47}{14},\frac{47}{14}\right)\).

4. **Find the radius** by plugging \(h\) into one of the distance equations. Use the point \((1,2)\):  
   $$
   r^{2}=\left(1-\frac{47}{14}\right)^{2}+\left(2-\frac{47}{14}\right)^{2}
   =\left(\frac{-33}{14}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{-19}{14}\right)^{2}
   =\frac{1089+361}{196}
   =\frac{1450}{196}
   =\frac{725}{98}.
   $$  
   So \(r=\sqrt{\frac{725}{98}}=\frac{\sqrt{725}}{7}\).

5. **Write the standard form** using centre \((h,k)\) and radius \(r\).  
   $$
   \left(x-\frac{47}{14}\right)^{2}+\left(y-\frac{47}{14}\right)^{2}= \frac{725}{98}.
   $$

**Answer:** The required circle is \(\displaystyle\left(x-\frac{47}{14}\right)^{2}+\left(y-\frac{47}{14}\right)^{2}= \frac{725}{98}\); its centre is \(\bigl(\frac{47}{14},\frac{47}{14}\bigr)\) and its radius is \(\frac{\sqrt{725}}{7}\).

> **In daily life:** Completing the square is like rearranging furniture in a room so that the centre of the circle becomes the new “origin” of the space; everything else is measured relative to that point.  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to add the same constant to both sides of the equation when completing the square. This changes the balance and gives an incorrect radius.  

By mastering these steps, any circle given in general form can be rewritten in the clear, geometric language of centre and radius. This makes further work—such as graphing, intersecting with lines, or solving word problems—much easier.

sections.heading: 5. Word Problems Involving Circle Equations
sections.body:
When we meet a word problem that talks about a round object – a fountain, a fence, a radar dish, a satellite – the first thing to do is to turn the description into a circle equation.  
The equation then lets us answer questions such as “how far must we stay away?” or “how long does one revolution take?”.  

> **In daily life:**  A circle equation is a compact way of keeping track of every point that is the same distance from a fixed centre.  

---

**Example 7 (Level 1): Walking path inside a circular park**  
A circular park has its centre at $(-2,5)$ and a fence that is $20\,$m from the centre. Inside the fence there is a walking path that stays $3\,$m away from the fence. Write the equation of the walking path.

1. **Find the radius of the fence.**  
   The distance from the centre to the fence is given as $20\,$m, so the fence radius $R$ is  
   $$R = 20.$$  

2. **Determine the radius of the walking path.**  
   The path is $3\,$m inside the fence, therefore its radius $r$ is the fence radius minus $3\,$m:  
   $$r = R - 3 = 20 - 3 = 17.$$  

3. **Write the equation in centre‑radius (standard) form.**  
   For a circle with centre $(h,k)$ and radius $r$ the standard form is  
   $$(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2.$$  
   Substituting $h=-2$, $k=5$, and $r=17$ gives  
   $$(x+2)^2 + (y-5)^2 = 17^2.$$  

**Answer:** The walking path is described by  
$$(x+2)^2 + (y-5)^2 = 289,$$  
where every point on the path is $17\,$m from the centre $(-2,5)$.  

---

**Example 8 (Level 2): Satellite orbit and its period**  
A satellite moves in a circular orbit with centre at the origin $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(0,-10)$. The satellite travels at a constant speed of $2\,$km/s. Write the orbit’s equation and state its period (time for one full revolution).

1. **Find the radius of the orbit.**  
   Any point on the circle is the same distance from the centre. The distance from $(0,0)$ to $(0,-10)$ is $10\,$km, so the radius $r$ is  
   $$r = 10.$$  

2. **Write the standard form of the orbit.**  
   With centre $(0,0)$ the equation simplifies to  
   $$x^2 + y^2 = r^2 = 10^2 = 100.$$  

3. **Compute the period using the circumference.**  
   The distance travelled in one revolution is the circumference $C = 2\pi r$.  
   $$C = 2\pi(10) = 20\pi\ \text{km}.$$  
   Speed $v = 2\,$km/s, so time $T = \dfrac{C}{v}$:  
   $$T = \frac{20\pi}{2} = 10\pi\ \text{s} \approx 31.4\ \text{s}.$$  

**Answer:** The satellite’s orbit is  
$$x^2 + y^2 = 100,$$  
and it completes one revolution every $10\pi\,$seconds (about $31.4\,$s).  

---

Now let’s see how the same steps work for a slightly different situation.

> **Definition:** *Completing the square* is the algebraic process that rewrites a quadratic expression $ax^2+bx+c$ as $a(x-h)^2+k$, revealing the centre $(h,k)$ and radius $\sqrt{k}$ of a circle.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to move the constant term to the other side before completing the square, which leads to an incorrect radius.

**Worked idea:** Suppose a problem tells you that a radar dish is $5\,$m from a control tower and the safe zone is a circle that stays $2\,$m away from the dish. The dish itself is centred at $(3, -4)$.  

1. **Radius of the dish** is $5\,$m, so the safe zone radius is $5+2 = 7\,$m.  
2. **Write the standard form** using centre $(3,-4)$ and radius $7$:  
   $$(x-3)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 7^2 = 49.$$  

If the problem instead gave the equation $x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 8y + 9 = 0$, we would **complete the square**:

1. Group $x$‑terms and $y$‑terms: $x^2 - 6x \;+\; y^2 + 8y = -9$.  
2. Add and subtract the needed squares inside the equation:  
   $$\bigl(x^2 - 6x + 9\bigr) + \bigl(y^2 + 8y + 16\bigr) = -9 + 9 + 16.$$  
3. Rewrite as perfect squares:  
   $$(x-3)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 16.$$  

Thus the centre is $(3,-4)$ and the radius is $4\,$m.  

> **Remember:** After completing the square, the right‑hand side must be a positive number; otherwise the “circle” does not exist in the real plane.

These examples show the full pipeline for word problems:

1. **Read the story** and identify the centre and any distances mentioned.  
2. **Translate distances** into a radius (add or subtract as the problem says “inside” or “outside”).  
3. **Write the standard form** $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$.  
4. **If needed, expand** to general form or **complete the square** to go back to centre‑radius form.  
5. **Interpret the result** – the equation tells you every point that satisfies the condition, and you can use it to compute further quantities such as perimeter, area, or time for one revolution.

By practising these steps with real‑world contexts, you will become comfortable turning any description of a round object into a precise mathematical equation, and then using that equation to answer practical questions.

practice.q: Write the standard form of a circle with centre $(-2,3)$ and radius $4$.
Expand the standard form $(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=9$ to general form.
Find the centre and radius of the circle given by $x^2+y^2-6x+8y+9=0$.
A circle passes through the points $A(1,2)$ and $B(5,6)$ and has centre on the line $x+y=4$. Find its equation.
practice.a:
Let centre be $(h,k)$ with $h+k=4$.
Distance to $A$: $(1-h)^2+(2-k)^2 = r^2$.
Distance to $B$: $(5-h)^2+(6-k)^2 = r^2$.
Set them equal and simplify:
\[
(1-h)^2+(2-k)^2 = (5-h)^2+(6-k)^2 \\
\Rightarrow (1-h)^2-(5-h)^2 + (2-k)^2-(6-k)^2 =0 \\
\Rightarrow [(1-h)-(5-h)][(1-h)+(5-h)] + [(2-k)-(6-k)][(2-k)+(6-k)] =0 \\
\Rightarrow (-4)(6-2h) + (-4)(8-2k)=0 \\
\Rightarrow -24+8h -32+8k =0 \\
\Rightarrow 8h+8k =56 \\
\Rightarrow h+k =7.
\]
But we also have $h+k=4$, a contradiction, so no such circle exists. (Thus the problem is impossible; the given conditions are inconsistent.)

practice.q: Convert the general equation $2x^2+2y^2-8x+12y-10=0$ to standard form and state the centre and radius.

A circular track has equation $x^2+y^2+10x-24y+139=0$. A runner starts at the point on the circle directly east of the centre and runs counter‑clockwise for a quarter of the circumference. Find the coordinates of the runner’s final position.
practice.a:
Complete the square to locate the centre:
\[
x^2+10x + y^2-24y = -139 \\
(x+5)^2-25 + (y-12)^2-144 = -139 \\
(x+5)^2+(y-12)^2 = 30.
\]
Centre $C(-5,12)$, radius $r=\sqrt{30}$.
The “east” point has the same $y$‑coordinate as the centre and $x$ increased by $r$:
\[
P_0 = ( -5 + \sqrt{30},\; 12).
\]
A quarter turn counter‑clockwise rotates the radius vector $90^\circ$; the vector from centre to $P_0$ is $(\sqrt{30},0)$. Rotating $90^\circ$ CCW gives $(0,\sqrt{30})$. Add to centre:
\[
P_{\text{final}} = (-5 + 0,\; 12 + \sqrt{30}) = (-5,\; 12+\sqrt{30}).
\]
Thus the runner’s final coordinates are $\displaystyle\bigl(-5,\;12+\sqrt{30}\bigr)$.

data.recap: A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance (radius) from a centre (h,k). Its standard equation is (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2, which comes from the distance formula. General form expands this to x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F=0, and completing the square reveals the hidden centre and radius. These tools let us write and solve real‑world problems involving circles.

quiz.q: What is the definition of a circle in the coordinate plane?
options: All points whose x‑coordinates are equal
All points at a fixed distance from a centre
quiz.why: A circle consists of points exactly r units from a centre (h,k).

quiz.why: Standard form isolates the centre (h,k) and radius r.

quiz.q: If a circle has centre (3,-2) and radius 5, what is its equation in standard form?
What is the first step in completing the square for x^2+6x?

quiz.q: A circle in general form is x^2+y^2-4x+8y-12=0. What is its centre?
quiz.why: Completing the square gives (x-2)^2+(y+4)^2=36, so centre is (2,-4).

quiz.q: Why do we square both sides of the distance formula when deriving the circle equation?
quiz.why: Squaring removes the square root, yielding a polynomial equation.

data.title: Tangent and Normal to a Circle
data.summary: In this lesson students learn how to find the equations of tangents and normals to a circle and understand their geometric meaning. They will practice deriving these equations using the circle’s centre and radius.
objectives: Derive the slope of a tangent line to a circle at a given point
Write the equation of a tangent line in point‑slope and general form
Derive and write the equation of the normal line at a point on the circle
Apply the tangent and normal equations to solve geometry problems
data.prerequisites: Students should know the standard equation of a circle (x‑h)²+(y‑k)²=r² and basic slope‑intercept form of a line.
why: Tangents model real‑world situations where a straight object just touches a curved surface, such as a road meeting a circular roundabout or a light ray grazing a lens.
Normals are used in engineering and physics to describe forces acting perpendicular to surfaces, for example the direction of a normal force on a wheel or the gradient of a hill.

sections.heading: Review: Circle Equation and Slope
sections.body:
A circle is a set of all points that are the same distance from a single centre point.  
If the centre is at the coordinates $(h,k)$ and the common distance (called the **radius**) is $r$, every point $(x,y)$ on the circle satisfies  

$$ (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^{2}. $$  

> **Definition:** The equation $ (x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^{2}$ is called the *standard form* of a circle.  
> It tells us exactly where the centre $(h,k)$ is and how long the radius $r$ is.

Why does this work?  Imagine you have a nail at the centre $(h,k)$ and a string of length $r$ tied to the nail.  If you pull the string taut and move a pencil around while keeping the string tight, the pencil tip traces a perfect circle.  Every position of the pencil is a point $(x,y)$ whose distance to the nail is exactly $r$.  The distance formula between two points $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ is  

$$ \text{distance}= \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}. $$  

Setting this distance equal to $r$ and squaring both sides removes the square‑root, giving the standard form above.

---

When we talk about the **slope** of a line, we are measuring how steep the line is.  For a line that passes through two distinct points $P_1=(x_1,y_1)$ and $P_2=(x_2,y_2)$, the slope $m$ is  

$$ m = \frac{y_2-y_1}{\,x_2-x_1\,}. $$  

> **Note:** The denominator $x_2-x_1$ must not be zero.  If it is zero, the line is vertical and its slope is undefined (or we say it is “infinite”).

Think of slope as the “rise over run” you hear about when climbing a hill.  If you walk from $P_1$ to $P_2$, the “rise” is the change in the vertical direction $y_2-y_1$, and the “run” is the change in the horizontal direction $x_2-x_1$.  A larger rise compared to run means a steeper hill (larger slope); a flat road has rise $0$, giving slope $0$.

Why do we need the slope when studying circles?  Later we will look at lines that just touch a circle (tangents) or cut straight through it (normals).  Those lines are described by their slopes, and the relationship between the slope of a line and the slope of a radius drawn to the point of contact is essential.  Knowing how to compute a slope quickly lets us write the equation of any line that interacts with the circle.

Let’s see a quick example.  Suppose we have a circle centred at $(2,3)$ with radius $5$, so its equation is  

$$ (x-2)^2 + (y-3)^2 = 25. $$  

Pick two points on the circle, say $A=(7,3)$ and $B=(2,8)$.  The slope of the line $AB$ is  

$$ m_{AB}= \frac{8-3}{2-7}= \frac{5}{-5}= -1. $$  

Notice that $A$ lies directly to the right of the centre (same $y$‑coordinate), while $B$ lies directly above the centre (same $x$‑coordinate).  The line $AB$ is not a radius; it is a chord.  Its slope $-1$ tells us the line falls one unit vertically for each unit it moves horizontally to the left.

> **Remember:** Always subtract the coordinates in the same order: $y_2-y_1$ over $x_2-x_1$.  Swapping the order changes the sign of the slope but still describes the same line.

Understanding the standard circle equation and the slope formula gives us the tools to describe any line that meets the circle, whether it just grazes the edge (tangent) or cuts straight through (secant).  These basics will be the foundation for the next part of the lesson, where we explore the special perpendicular relationship between a radius and a tangent line.

sections.heading: Concept: Tangent Line as Perpendicular to Radius
sections.body:
When a line just touches a circle at one single point, we call that line a **tangent**.  
Imagine the circle as a smooth round table and the tangent as a thin ruler that leans against the edge without cutting through it. At the exact spot where the ruler meets the edge, the edge (the circle’s **radius**) points straight out from the centre, while the ruler lies flat against the edge. Because the ruler does not go inside the circle, the two directions are at right angles to each other.

> **Definition:** *At the point of contact between a circle and its tangent, the radius drawn to that point is perpendicular (forms a $90^\circ$ angle) to the tangent line.*

Why does this happen?  
Think of a wheel rolling on a flat road. The point of the wheel that touches the road does not slip; the road is tangent to the wheel there. The wheel’s axle (the radius to the touching point) points directly toward the centre of the wheel, while the road runs straight ahead. The two directions cannot share any component; otherwise the wheel would either dig into the road or lift off. This geometric fact is true for any circle, no matter its size or position.

### From perpendicularity to slope

In the coordinate plane we describe a line by its **slope** $m$, the ratio “rise over run”. Two lines are perpendicular exactly when the product of their slopes is $-1$:

$$ m_1 \, m_2 = -1. $$

If we know the slope of the radius at the point of contact, we can immediately obtain the slope of the tangent by solving this equation for $m_{\text{tangent}}$.

The radius that joins the centre $(h,k)$ of the circle to a point $(x_0,y_0)$ on the circle has slope

$$ m_{\text{radius}} = \frac{y_0-k}{\,x_0-h\,}. $$

Therefore the tangent slope $m_T$ satisfies

$$ m_T \cdot \frac{y_0-k}{\,x_0-h\,} = -1, $$

so

$$ m_T = -\frac{x_0-h}{\,y_0-k\,}. $$

Notice how the numerator and denominator have swapped places and a minus sign appears – that is the algebraic expression of “turning $90^\circ$”.

> **Note:** The formula $m_T = -\dfrac{x_0-h}{y_0-k}$ works for any circle $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ and any point $(x_0,y_0)$ on it, provided $y_0\neq k$ (the radius is not vertical). If the radius is vertical, the tangent is horizontal, and its slope is $0$.

Now we can use this slope together with the point $(x_0,y_0)$ to write the tangent line in point‑slope form:

$$ y - y_0 = m_T\,(x - x_0). $$

That equation describes the straight line that just grazes the circle at $(x_0,y_0)$.

---

**Example 1 (Easy): Find the slope of the tangent to $(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2=9$ at the point $(5,1)$.**

1. **Identify centre and radius.**  
   The given equation matches the standard form $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ with  
   $$h=2,\qquad k=-1,\qquad r=3.$$

2. **Compute the slope of the radius.**  
   Use the two points: centre $(2,-1)$ and point of contact $(5,1)$.  
   $$ m_{\text{radius}} = \frac{1-(-1)}{5-2} = \frac{2}{3}. $$

3. **Find the tangent slope using perpendicularity.**  
   Set $m_T \cdot m_{\text{radius}} = -1$:  
   $$ m_T \cdot \frac{2}{3} = -1 \;\Longrightarrow\; m_T = -\frac{3}{2}. $$

**Answer:** The tangent at $(5,1)$ has slope $m_T = -\dfrac{3}{2}$.

---

With the slope known, the full tangent line can be written if needed:

$$ y-1 = -\frac{3}{2}\,(x-5). $$

> **In daily life:** When a car’s wheel touches the road, the direction the road runs (the tangent) is perpendicular to the line from the wheel’s centre to the contact point (the radius). Engineers use this fact to design smooth transitions between road segments.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to use the negative reciprocal when converting the radius slope to the tangent slope. Remember, perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$, not simply “swap places”.

> **Remember:** Always verify that the point you are using really lies on the circle. Plugging $(x_0,y_0)$ into $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ should give $r^2$; otherwise the slope you compute does not correspond to a true tangent.

sections.heading: Formula: Tangent Equation Using Point‑Slope
sections.body:
When we want the line that just touches a circle at a single point, we call it the **tangent**.  
The word *tangent* comes from the Latin *tangere*, meaning “to touch”.  
At the point of contact the tangent line does not cut through the circle; it only “grazes” it.  

> **Definition:** A tangent line to a circle is a straight line that meets the circle at exactly one point.

Why does the tangent have a special slope?  
Think of the radius that joins the centre of the circle to the point where the tangent touches. If you draw the radius and the tangent together, they form a right angle (they are *perpendicular*). This is a fundamental property of circles: the radius is always perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.

> **Note:** Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other. If one line has slope $m$, a line perpendicular to it has slope $-\dfrac{1}{m}$ (provided $m\neq0$).

Because we know the slope of the radius, we can immediately find the slope of the tangent.  
Suppose the circle has centre $(h,k)$ and the point of tangency is $(x_1,y_1)$.  
The radius joins $(h,k)$ to $(x_1,y_1)$, so its slope $m_r$ is  

$$
m_r=\frac{y_1-k}{\,x_1-h\,}.
$$

The tangent slope $m_t$ is the negative reciprocal of $m_r$:

$$
m_t=-\frac{1}{m_r}= -\frac{x_1-h}{\,y_1-k\,}.
$$

Now we have the slope of the tangent line and we also know a point that lies on it – the very point of tangency $(x_1,y_1)$.  
With a point and a slope we can write the line in **point‑slope form**:

$$
y-y_1=m_t\,(x-x_1).
$$

This formula is the tool we will use for any circle, no matter where its centre is located.

> **In daily life:** Imagine a bike wheel rolling on a flat road. The road is the tangent to the wheel at the point where the wheel touches the ground. The wheel’s radius points straight up from that contact point, forming a right angle with the road.

---

**Example 2 (Medium): Write the equation of the tangent to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ at $(4,0)$.**  

1. Identify the centre and radius of the circle.  
   The equation $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ can be written as $(x-0)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}=4^{2}$, so the centre is $(h,k)=(0,0)$ and the radius is $4$.  

2. Compute the slope of the radius through $(4,0)$.  
   $$m_r=\frac{0-0}{4-0}=0.$$

3. Find the tangent slope as the negative reciprocal of $m_r$.  
   Since $m_r=0$, the radius is horizontal, so the tangent must be vertical. A vertical line has an undefined slope, but we can describe it directly as $x=4$.  

4. Write the tangent equation using point‑slope (or directly for a vertical line).  
   Because the line is vertical, the equation is simply  

   $$x=4.$$

**Answer:** The tangent to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ at the point $(4,0)$ is the vertical line $x=4$.

---

**Example 3 (Medium): Find the tangent to $(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=25$ at $(8,2)$.**  

1. Read the centre and radius from the equation.  
   The circle is centred at $(h,k)=(3,2)$ with radius $5$ because $(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=5^{2}$.  

2. Determine the slope of the radius joining $(3,2)$ to the point $(8,2)$.  
   $$m_r=\frac{2-2}{\,8-3\,}=0.$$

3. Obtain the tangent slope as the negative reciprocal of $m_r$.  
   Again $m_r=0$, so the tangent is a vertical line. Its slope is undefined, and the line passes through $x=8$.  

4. Write the tangent equation.  
   $$x=8.$$

**Answer:** The tangent to the circle $(x-3)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=25$ at the point $(8,2)$ is the vertical line $x=8$.

> **Remember:** Whenever the radius at the point of tangency is horizontal (slope $0$) or vertical (undefined slope), the tangent line will be the opposite: vertical or horizontal respectively. In those cases you can write the tangent equation directly as $x=$ constant or $y=$ constant without using the point‑slope algebra.

With the point‑slope formula $y-y_1=m_t(x-x_1)$, we can now handle any situation where the radius has a non‑zero, finite slope. The steps are always:

1. Find the centre $(h,k)$ of the circle.  
2. Compute the radius slope $m_r=\dfrac{y_1-k}{x_1-h}$.  
3. Take the negative reciprocal to get $m_t=-\dfrac{x_1-h}{y_1-k}$.  
4. Plug $m_t$ and $(x_1,y_1)$ into $y-y_1=m_t(x-x_1)$.

Following these small, clear steps guarantees the correct tangent line every time.

sections.heading: Normal Line: Perpendicular to Tangent
sections.body:
When we talk about the **normal line** to a circle we mean the straight line that meets the circle at a single point and is **perpendicular** (forms a right‑angle) to the tangent line at that same point.  

Why does this matter?  
If you picture a wheel rolling on the ground, the point where the wheel touches the road is the point of tangency. The direction the wheel pushes straight into the ground is along the normal. In many geometry problems we need the normal because it tells us the direction of the radius, and the radius is often the key to distances, angles, or forces.

---

> **Definition:** The normal line at a point on a circle passes through that point and has slope  

$$m_n = -\frac{1}{m_t}$$  

where $m_t$ is the slope of the tangent line at the same point.  

> **Note:** Two lines are perpendicular exactly when the product of their slopes equals $-1$; that is, $m_1\,m_2 = -1$.

> **In daily life:** Think of a flagpole standing on a circular base. The pole is the normal (it points straight out from the centre), while a rope wrapped tightly around the base at the contact point would be tangent (it just grazes the circle).

> **Remember:** The normal always goes through the centre of the circle, because the radius is a normal line.

---

### Deriving the slope of the normal

1. **Find the slope of the radius.**  
   For a circle with centre $(h,k)$ and a point of contact $P(x_0,y_0)$ on the circle, the radius is the segment joining $(h,k)$ to $(x_0,y_0)$. Its slope is  

   $$m_r = \frac{y_0-k}{x_0-h}.$$

2. **Use the relationship between radius and tangent.**  
   The tangent line at $P$ is perpendicular to the radius, so  

   $$m_t \, m_r = -1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_t = -\frac{1}{m_r}.$$

3. **Find the slope of the normal.**  
   The normal is the same line as the radius, so its slope $m_n$ equals $m_r$. Substituting $m_r = -\frac{1}{m_t}$ gives  

   $$m_n = -\frac{1}{m_t}.$$

Thus the normal’s slope is simply the negative reciprocal of the tangent’s slope, and it passes through the same point $P(x_0,y_0)$.

---

### Writing the equation of the normal

Once we know $m_n$ and the point $P$, we can use the point‑slope form of a line:

$$y - y_0 = m_n\,(x - x_0).$$

This compact formula gives the normal line directly.

---

**Example 4 (Medium): Determine the equation of the normal to $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ at $(3,4)$.**  

1. *Identify the centre and radius.*  
   The circle is centred at the origin $(0,0)$ with radius $5$.  

2. *Compute the slope of the radius (which is the normal).*  
   $$m_n = \frac{4-0}{3-0} = \frac{4}{3}.$$

3. *Write the normal using point‑slope.*  
   $$y - 4 = \frac{4}{3}\,(x - 3).$$  

   Simplify if desired:  

   $$3(y-4)=4(x-3) \;\Longrightarrow\; 3y-12 = 4x-12 \;\Longrightarrow\; 4x-3y = 0.$$

**Answer:** The normal line is $4x-3y=0$, or equivalently $y-4=\frac{4}{3}(x-3)$.

---

**Example 5 (Hard): For the circle $(x+1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=13$, find both tangent and normal equations at the point $(2,5)$.**  

1. *Locate the centre.*  
   The centre is $C(-1,2)$.  

2. *Find the slope of the radius (normal).*  
   $$m_n = \frac{5-2}{2-(-1)} = \frac{3}{3}=1.$$

3. *Write the normal equation using point‑slope.*  
   $$y-5 = 1\,(x-2) \;\Longrightarrow\; y = x+3.$$

4. *Obtain the slope of the tangent as the negative reciprocal of $m_n$.*  
   $$m_t = -\frac{1}{m_n} = -1.$$

5. *Write the tangent equation through $(2,5)$.*  
   $$y-5 = -1\,(x-2) \;\Longrightarrow\; y-5 = -x+2 \;\Longrightarrow\; x+y = 7.$$

**Answer:**  
- Normal line: $y = x + 3$ (or $y-5 = x-2$).  
- Tangent line: $x + y = 7$ (or $y-5 = - (x-2)$).

These two lines intersect at the given point $(2,5)$ and are perpendicular, confirming the relationship $m_n\,m_t = -1$.

---

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the normal passes through the centre of the circle. If you use a point other than the centre to compute $m_n$, the line will not be perpendicular to the tangent.

By always starting with the radius, computing its slope, and then applying the negative‑reciprocal rule, you can quickly write both tangent and normal equations for any circle. This technique is a staple in analytic geometry and appears in physics (forces on a curved surface), engineering (design of gears), and everyday problem‑solving.

sections.heading: Applications: Solving Geometry Problems
sections.body:
When we know the equation of a tangent or a normal line to a circle, we can use it just like any other straight‑line equation: we can find where it meets another line, calculate distances, or check whether a point really lies on the line. This turns many geometry puzzles into simple algebra problems.

> **Note:** A *tangent* touches the circle at exactly one point, while a *normal* passes through the centre and meets the circle at a right angle to the tangent.

The power of these ideas becomes clear when we apply them to real‑world‑style questions. Below we work through two challenging problems step by step, showing how the tangent‑and‑normal formulas do the heavy lifting.

---

**Example 6 (Hard): Road tangent to a circle**  
A road is tangent to the circle \((x-6)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=36\) at point \(P\). The road also passes through the origin \((0,0)\). Find the coordinates of \(P\).

1. **Write the centre and radius of the circle.**  
   The centre is \(C(6,-3)\) and the radius is \(r=6\) because the equation is of the form \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\).

2. **Use the fact that the radius \(CP\) is perpendicular to the tangent line.**  
   If the road is tangent at \(P(x_{P},y_{P})\), then the slope of \(CP\) times the slope of the road equals \(-1\).

   The slope of \(CP\) is  
   $$m_{CP}= \frac{y_{P}+3}{x_{P}-6}.$$

   Let the slope of the road be \(m\). Because the road passes through \((0,0)\) and \(P\), its slope is also  
   $$m=\frac{y_{P}}{x_{P}}.$$

   Perpendicular condition:  
   $$m_{CP}\,m = -1.$$

3. **Set up the equations and solve for \(x_{P},y_{P}\).**  
   Substitute the two expressions for the slopes into the perpendicular condition:

   $$\frac{y_{P}+3}{x_{P}-6}\cdot\frac{y_{P}}{x_{P}} = -1.$$

   Multiply both sides by \(x_{P}(x_{P}-6)\):

   $$y_{P}(y_{P}+3) = -x_{P}(x_{P}-6).$$

   Expand:

   $$y_{P}^{2}+3y_{P} = -x_{P}^{2}+6x_{P}.$$

   Bring all terms to one side:

   $$x_{P}^{2}+y_{P}^{2}+3y_{P}-6x_{P}=0.\tag{1}$$

   Because \(P\) lies on the circle, it also satisfies  

   $$(x_{P}-6)^{2}+(y_{P}+3)^{2}=36.\tag{2}$$

   Expand (2):

   $$x_{P}^{2}-12x_{P}+36 + y_{P}^{2}+6y_{P}+9 = 36,$$
   $$x_{P}^{2}+y_{P}^{2}-12x_{P}+6y_{P}+9 = 0.\tag{3}$$

   Subtract equation (1) from equation (3):

   $$(x_{P}^{2}+y_{P}^{2}-12x_{P}+6y_{P}+9) - (x_{P}^{2}+y_{P}^{2}+3y_{P}-6x_{P}) = 0,$$
   $$-12x_{P}+6y_{P}+9 -3y_{P}+6x_{P}=0,$$
   $$-6x_{P}+3y_{P}+9=0,$$
   $$3y_{P}=6x_{P}-9,$$
   $$y_{P}=2x_{P}-3.$$

   Substitute \(y_{P}=2x_{P}-3\) into (1):

   $$x_{P}^{2}+(2x_{P}-3)^{2}+3(2x_{P}-3)-6x_{P}=0,$$
   $$x_{P}^{2}+4x_{P}^{2}-12x_{P}+9+6x_{P}-9-6x_{P}=0,$$
   $$5x_{P}^{2}-12x_{P}=0,$$
   $$x_{P}(5x_{P}-12)=0.$$

   The solution \(x_{P}=0\) would give the origin, which is not on the circle, so we take  

   $$5x_{P}-12=0 \;\Rightarrow\; x_{P}= \frac{12}{5}=2.4.$$

   Then  

   $$y_{P}=2(2.4)-3 = 4.8-3 = 1.8.$$

**Answer:** The point of tangency is \(P\left(\frac{12}{5},\frac{9}{5}\right) = (2.4,\;1.8)\). The road’s equation is \(y = \frac{1.8}{2.4}x = \frac{3}{4}x\).

---

> **In daily life:** Imagine a straight fence that just grazes a circular garden. The fence is a tangent; the line from the garden’s centre to the touching point is a normal. Knowing one tells you the other instantly.

---

**Example 7 (Hard): Common tangent to two circles**  
Two circles intersect. Find the equation of the common tangent that touches the first circle at \((1,\sqrt{3})\) and the second circle at \((4,2)\).

1. **Write the equations of the two circles.**  
   The first circle passes through \((1,\sqrt{3})\) and we are not given its centre, but we only need the tangent line. The second circle also passes through \((4,2)\). Because a tangent line is determined by a single point on each circle, we can directly use the point‑slope form.

2. **Find the slope of the tangent using the two points of tangency.**  
   The line that touches both circles must pass through both given points, so its slope \(m\) is

   $$m = \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{4-1} = \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{3}.$$

3. **Write the equation of the line using point‑slope form.**  
   Using point \((1,\sqrt{3})\):

   $$y-\sqrt{3}= m\,(x-1).$$

   Substitute \(m\):

   $$y-\sqrt{3}= \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{3}\,(x-1).$$

   Multiply out to obtain a tidy form:

   $$3(y-\sqrt{3}) = (2-\sqrt{3})(x-1).$$

   Expand:

   $$3y-3\sqrt{3}= (2-\sqrt{3})x-(2-\sqrt{3}).$$

   Bring all terms to one side:

   $$(2-\sqrt{3})x -3y +\bigl[3\sqrt{3}-(2-\sqrt{3})\bigr]=0.$$

   Simplify the constant:

   $$3\sqrt{3}-(2-\sqrt{3}) = 3\sqrt{3}-2+\sqrt{3}=4\sqrt{3}-2.$$

   Hence the tangent line is  

   $$ (2-\sqrt{3})x - 3y + (4\sqrt{3}-2)=0.$$

4. **Verify that the line is indeed tangent to each circle.**  
   For a line \(Ax+By+C=0\) and a circle \((x-h)^{2}+(y-k)^{2}=r^{2}\), the distance from the centre \((h,k)\) to the line must equal the radius \(r\).  
   Without the explicit centres we can check directly that each point of tangency satisfies the line equation:

   - At \((1,\sqrt{3})\):

     $$(2-\sqrt{3})\cdot1 -3\sqrt{3} + (4\sqrt{3}-2)=0,$$
     $$2-\sqrt{3}-3\sqrt{3}+4\sqrt{3}-2=0,$$
     $$0=0.$$

   - At \((4,2)\):

     $$(2-\sqrt{3})\cdot4 -3\cdot2 + (4\sqrt{3}-2)=0,$$
     $$8-4\sqrt{3}-6+4\sqrt{3}-2=0,$$
     $$0=0.$$

   Both points satisfy the line, confirming it touches each circle exactly once.

**Answer:** The common tangent is  

$$ (2-\sqrt{3})x - 3y + (4\sqrt{3}-2)=0,$$

or, equivalently,  

$$ y = \frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{3}\,x + \frac{4\sqrt{3}-2}{3}. $$

---

> **Remember:** To find a tangent line that meets two circles, you only need the coordinates of the two points of contact; the line through them automatically satisfies the tangency condition.

These examples show how turning geometric ideas into algebraic equations lets us solve seemingly tough problems with a clear, step‑by‑step procedure. Once you master the tangent and normal formulas, many geometry puzzles become routine calculations.

practice.q: Find the equation of the tangent line to the circle $(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2=9$ at the point $P(5,-1)$.
practice.a:
1. Identify centre $O=(2,-1)$ and radius $r=3$.
2. Compute slope of radius $OP$: $m_{\text{radius}}=\frac{-1-(-1)}{5-2}=0$.
3. Tangent slope $m_{\text{tangent}}=-\frac{1}{0}$ → vertical line, so $x=5$.
4. Equation of tangent: $\boxed{x=5}$.

practice.q: For the circle $x^2+y^2=16$, write the equation of the normal line at the point $Q(0,4)$.
practice.a:
1. Centre $O=(0,0)$.
2. Slope of radius $OQ$: $m_{\text{radius}}=\frac{4-0}{0-0}$ → undefined (vertical).
3. Normal line is the radius itself, a vertical line through $x=0$.
4. Equation of normal: $\boxed{x=0}$.

practice.q: Determine the equation of the tangent to the circle $(x+3)^2+(y-2)^2=25$ at the point $R(-3,7)$.
practice.a:
1. Centre $O=(-3,2)$, radius $5$.
2. Slope of radius $OR$: $m_{\text{radius}}=\frac{7-2}{-3-(-3)}=\frac{5}{0}$ → undefined (vertical).
3. Therefore tangent is horizontal: $y=7$.
4. Equation of tangent: $\boxed{y=7}$.

practice.q: A line $L$ passes through the point $S(1,2)$ and is tangent to the circle $x^2+y^2=5$. Find the equation(s) of $L$.
practice.a:
1. Let the slope of $L$ be $m$. Equation: $y-2=m(x-1)$.
2. Substitute $y = m(x-1)+2$ into circle: $x^2+[m(x-1)+2]^2=5$.
3. Expand and collect terms:
$x^2 + m^2(x-1)^2 +4m(x-1)+4 =5$.
This is a quadratic in $x$: $[1+m^2]x^2 +[-2m^2+4m]x +[m^2-4m+4-5]=0$.
4. For tangency, discriminant $=0$:
$(-2m^2+4m)^2 -4(1+m^2)(m^2-4m-1)=0$.
5. Simplify (after algebra) gives $m^2-4m+1=0$.
6. Solve: $m = \frac{4\pm\sqrt{16-4}}{2}= \frac{4\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}=2\pm\sqrt{3}$.
7. Therefore two tangent lines:
\[
y-2=(2+\sqrt3)(x-1)\quad\text{and}\quad y-2=(2-\sqrt3)(x-1).
\]

practice.q: Find the points on the circle $(x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=20$ where the tangent line has slope $-2$.
practice.a:
1. Let a generic point $P(x_0,y_0)$ lie on the circle, so $(x_0-1)^2+(y_0+2)^2=20$.
2. Slope of radius $OP$: $m_{\text{radius}}=\frac{y_0+2}{x_0-1}$.
3. Tangent slope $m_{\text{tangent}}=-\frac{1}{m_{\text{radius}}}$. Set this equal to $-2$:
\[
-\frac{1}{\frac{y_0+2}{x_0-1}} = -2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{x_0-1}{y_0+2}=2.
\]
Hence $x_0-1 = 2(y_0+2)$ → $x_0 = 2y_0+5$.
4. Substitute into circle equation:
\[
(2y_0+5-1)^2+(y_0+2)^2 =20 \\
(2y_0+4)^2+(y_0+2)^2 =20.
\]
Compute: $4y_0^2+16y_0+16 + y_0^2+4y_0+4 =20$.
Combine: $5y_0^2+20y_0+20=20 \;\Longrightarrow\; 5y_0^2+20y_0=0$.
Factor: $5y_0(y_0+4)=0$.
So $y_0=0$ or $y_0=-4$.
5. Corresponding $x_0$:
* If $y_0=0$, $x_0 = 2(0)+5 =5$.
* If $y_0=-4$, $x_0 = 2(-4)+5 = -3$.
6. Points are $\boxed{(5,0)}$ and $\boxed{(-3,-4)}$.

practice.q: A circle has centre $C(2, -3)$ and passes through the point $T(6,1)$. Find the equation of the normal line at $T$ and verify that it indeed passes through $C$.
practice.a:
1. Radius vector $\overrightarrow{CT} = (6-2,\;1-(-3)) = (4,4)$.
2. Slope of radius (and thus normal) $m_{\text{normal}} = \frac{4}{4}=1$.
3. Equation of normal using point $T(6,1)$:
\[
y-1 = 1\,(x-6) \;\Longrightarrow\; y = x-5.
\]
4. Check that $C(2,-3)$ satisfies $y = x-5$:
$-3 = 2-5 = -3$, true.
5. Hence normal line is $\boxed{y = x-5}$ and it passes through the centre as required.

data.recap: A circle is all points at a fixed distance r from a centre (h,k) and is written (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2. A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point. The normal line passes through the same point and is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is the negative reciprocal of the tangent slope. These ideas let us write equations for tangents and normals and solve geometry problems.

key_terms.meaning: Set of points at a constant distance (radius) from a fixed centre
Equation (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2 that shows centre (h,k) and radius r
A straight line that meets a circle at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius at that point
A line through the point of tangency that is perpendicular to the tangent; it aligns with the radius
Rise over run (change in y divided by change in x) that describes the steepness of a line
If a line has slope m, a line perpendicular to it has slope -1/m
Equation of a line y-y1=m(x-x1) using a known point (x1,y1) and slope m
Two lines are perpendicular when the product of their slopes equals -1

quiz.q: What is the standard form equation of a circle with centre (2,-3) and radius 5?
quiz.why: Plug centre and radius into (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2.

quiz.q: If a tangent to a circle at point (4,0) has slope 2, what is the slope of the normal line at that point?
quiz.why: Normal slope is the negative reciprocal of the tangent slope.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about a radius drawn to the point of tangency?
options: It is parallel to the tangent
It is perpendicular to the tangent
It has the same slope as the tangent
quiz.why: A radius is always perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.

quiz.q: For the circle (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=9, what is the slope of the tangent line at point (4,-2)?
quiz.why: The radius to (4,-2) is horizontal, so its slope is 0; the tangent is vertical, giving undefined slope. Actually radius slope is 0, so tangent slope is undefined.

quiz.q: What is the point‑slope form of the tangent line to a circle at point (x0,y0) with tangent slope mt?
quiz.why: Point‑slope form uses the point (x0,y0) and the line’s slope mt.

quiz.q: If two lines have slopes 3 and m and are perpendicular, what is m?
quiz.why: Perpendicular slopes satisfy m1*m2=-1, so m=-1/3.
